prompt: In a container, what is the highest layer that every program on the machine shares?
hint: Look at where the dashed line sits in the third stack.

choices.text: The kernel
choices.why: Right. Above the kernel, each container has its own files and libraries.

choices.text: The libraries installed on the host
choices.why: Each container brings its own libraries in its image; sharing them is the bare-metal arrangement.

choices.text: A hypervisor running under every container
choices.why: There is no hypervisor in the container stack; that belongs to virtual machines.

choices.text: Nothing at all, each container has its own copy of everything
choices.why: Each container still makes its system calls to the host's one kernel.

prompt: Bruno needs a Windows server and a Linux server on the same physical machine. Which arrangement allows it?
hint: Which stack gives each guest its own kernel?

choices.text: Two containers, one from a Windows image and one from a Linux image, on a Linux host
choices.why: A container uses the host's kernel, so on a Linux host every container is a Linux one.

choices.text: Bare metal with both operating systems installed side by side and running at once
choices.why: On bare metal one operating system owns the machine at a time.

choices.text: Two virtual machines on a hypervisor
choices.why: Right. Each VM boots its own kernel, so they can be different operating systems.

choices.text: Two containers with `--platform windows`
choices.why: `--platform` picks an image variant; it cannot supply a Windows kernel to a Linux host.

prompt: Match each piece to where it runs.
hint: Two hypervisors and one container engine.

pairs.left: Type 1 hypervisor, like KVM or ESXi
pairs.right: Directly on the hardware, under the guests
As a program on an ordinary operating system
As programs on the host's own kernel, with no guest kernel

right_distractors: Inside each container, one per container

prompt: A company runs its containers on cloud VMs. Which boundary separates it from another customer of the same provider?

choices.text: The container walls, since both customers use Docker
choices.why: Containers separate programs inside one customer's machine; the provider does not rely on them between customers.

choices.text: The hypervisor under the VMs
choices.why: Right. The provider separates customers with VMs and their hypervisor's stronger boundary.

choices.text: The kernel, which each customer shares with the other
choices.why: Each VM has its own kernel; two customers on one host do not share one.

choices.text: Nothing; the cloud gives every customer a separate physical building
choices.why: Customers share physical machines; the hypervisor is what keeps them apart.

prompt: On Ana's Ubuntu machine, `docker run --rm debian:trixie-slim uname -r` prints what?
hint: Which kernel answers the system call?

choices.text: The host's kernel release, the same as `uname -r` on the host
choices.why: Right: `6.18.44-fc-v70` three times. The image brings Debian's files, not a kernel.

choices.text: Debian 13's kernel release
choices.why: The image does not contain a running kernel; there is only the host's.

choices.text: Nothing, because a container has no kernel to report
choices.why: The call reaches the host's kernel, which answers.

choices.text: An error, since Debian cannot run on Ubuntu
choices.why: It ran: a Debian userland on the host's kernel is exactly what the image is.

prompt: What does an image named `alpine` give a container?

choices.text: Alpine's files: shell, libraries, package manager and `/etc`
choices.why: Right. The distribution is the files; the kernel is the host's.

choices.text: Alpine's kernel, which is smaller than Ubuntu's and therefore boots faster
choices.why: No kernel comes with the image, and nothing boots.

choices.text: A virtual machine running Alpine
choices.why: There is no VM; the container is a process on the host.

choices.text: A copy of the host's Ubuntu, renamed
choices.why: `/etc/os-release` inside says Alpine Linux v3.22, because the files are Alpine's.

prompt: Why can a Debian 13 `ls` run on a kernel that Debian 13 never shipped?
hint: What does a program need from the kernel?

choices.text: Docker recompiles every program in the image for the host's kernel
choices.why: Nothing is recompiled; the binaries in the image run as they are.

choices.text: Because the Linux kernel keeps its interface to programs stable across versions
choices.why: Right. A program built for one kernel's interface keeps working on later ones.

choices.text: Debian and Ubuntu share one kernel source
choices.why: Even an Alpine `ls`, from a different distribution family, runs on the same kernel.

choices.text: `ls` makes no system calls
choices.why: It reads directories, which is system calls; they just mean the same thing on every recent kernel.

prompt: In the transcript, how many seconds did `time docker run --rm alpine:3.22 true` take on the wall clock? Answer with the `real` value.
hint: The first of the three lines.

prompt: `docker stats` shows the idle container at `668KiB / 15.72GiB`. What is the 15.72GiB?

choices.text: Memory Docker reserved for the container when it started
choices.why: Nothing was reserved; containers do not set memory aside the way a VM does.

choices.text: The host's memory, because no limit was set
choices.why: Right. With no limit, the ceiling is everything the host has.

choices.text: The size of the alpine image on disk
choices.why: The image is 12.8MB on disk; this column is about memory.

choices.text: Memory used by all containers together
choices.why: The usage is the 668KiB on the left; the right side is the ceiling.

prompt: Inside a container started with `--memory 256m`, `free -m` reports about 16,000 MB. Why?
hint: Which file does `free` read, and what does it describe?

choices.text: The limit only takes effect after the first allocation
choices.why: The limit is in force from the start; `free` simply cannot see it.

choices.text: `--memory` is ignored on cgroup v1
choices.why: It is enforced; `docker stats` would show the limit.

choices.text: Alpine's `free` is broken
choices.why: Debian's or Ubuntu's would print the same number; the file is the host's.

choices.text: `free` reads `/proc/meminfo`, which describes the host's memory; the limit lives in a cgroup
choices.why: Right. The limit is real and invisible to anything that reads `/proc/meminfo`.

prompt: A program starts one worker thread per processor it counts with `nproc`. In a container with `--cpus 1` on Ana's 4-processor machine, how many workers does it start?
hint: What did `nproc` print inside that container?

choices.text: 1, because the container has exactly one processor available to it
choices.why: `--cpus 1` limits time, not what `nproc` reports; it printed 4.

choices.text: 4, and they then share one processor's worth of time
choices.why: Right. It sizes itself for the host and gets a quarter of what it planned for.

choices.text: 0, because `nproc` fails inside a container and the program falls back to none
choices.why: `nproc` answered 4 in the transcript.

choices.text: 2, half of the host
choices.why: Nothing halves it; the program sees the host's count.

prompt: `docker run --platform linux/arm64 alpine:3.22 uname -m` fails on Ana's `x86_64` machine with `exec format error`. What failed?

choices.text: The download of the image
choices.why: The image was found and unpacked; the failure came after that.

choices.text: Docker's permission check
choices.why: Permissions produce `permission denied`, a different message.

choices.text: The kernel could not execute an arm64 binary
choices.why: Right. The file is a program for another processor.

choices.text: Alpine has no arm64 variant, so Docker substituted an empty image
choices.why: Alpine publishes arm64; the binary in it was simply for the wrong processor.

prompt: A tool needs a kernel module the host does not have. Why can its container not simply bring the module in its image?
hint: Whose kernel would the module be loaded into?

choices.text: Images cannot hold files larger than a few megabytes
choices.why: Images hold gigabytes; size is not the problem.

choices.text: Loading one changes the host itself, for every container on it at once
choices.why: Right. There is no kernel of the container's own to extend.

choices.text: Modules only exist on Windows
choices.why: Linux has loadable kernel modules; the issue is whose kernel.

choices.text: Docker deletes `.ko` files when it builds
choices.why: Nothing deletes them; a container simply has no kernel of its own to load them into.

prompt: Match each need to the arrangement the lesson recommends for it.
hint: Ask what has to be separate: the kernel, or only the files.

pairs.left: Two parties who do not trust each other on one host
A program packaged once for laptop, CI and server
One large database using the whole machine
pairs.right: Bare metal, or one VM sized to the machine

right_distractors: A container running its own kernel

prompt: Why does a kernel flaw threaten containers more than VMs on the same host?
hint: Count the kernels each arrangement has.

choices.text: Containers have no walls at all, so anything running inside one reaches the host directly
choices.why: They do: namespaces and cgroups. The point is what those walls are made of.

choices.text: Every container's wall is the same shared kernel, so one flaw opens them all
choices.why: Right. A VM's guest has its own kernel and sits behind the hypervisor.

choices.text: VMs receive kernel patches automatically from the hypervisor, and containers do not
choices.why: Neither patches itself; the difference is structural.

choices.text: Containers run as root on the host
choices.why: They can, and lesson 14 changes that, but the shared kernel is the reason here.

prompt: On an Apple silicon Mac, an `amd64`-only image runs under Docker Desktop, but slowly. What is happening?

choices.text: Docker Desktop downloads an arm64 version from a different registry
choices.why: There is none for an amd64-only image; it runs the amd64 binary.

choices.text: The image is recompiled for arm64 on first run
choices.why: Nothing is recompiled; the instructions are translated as they run.

choices.text: Emulation
choices.why: Right. Each amd64 instruction is translated, which works and is slow.

choices.text: The Mac's kernel is x86_64 underneath
choices.why: It is arm64, which is exactly why the amd64 binary needs help.

prompt: Order these from the most to the least that each program carries for itself.
hint: Follow the line up the stacks.
items: A virtual machine: its own kernel, libraries and files
A container: its own libraries and files, the host's kernel
A program on bare metal: only its own binary, sharing the rest
